1.pericope_label: Go down to the house of the king of Judah: execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor; but if ye will not hear these words, I swear by myself that this house shall become a desolation

schools.summary: Places the message in the palace and in a particular reign, works the Hebrew of the charge for the exact force of its verbs and word order, and traces the rare oath formula and the promised chariots to their parallels elsewhere.

Takes the descent from the temple literally, reads the throne of David as an aggravation of guilt rather than a title of honour, and refuses to let the conditional promise be heard as a reprieve from the exile already determined.
Dates the oracle to the first year of the last reign, identifies the servants as the counsellors who advised rebellion, and reports the manuscript evidence behind the text.
Turns the visit into a maxim about authority and reduces the charge to two rules, that rulers do all the good their power allows and no hurt with it.

debates.question: Which king does the prophet confront?

positions.view: Jehoiakim, who was then reigning
Zedekiah, in the first year of his reign, the servants addressed being the ministers who had counselled him to rebel
the reigning king in his palace, but with the message reviewing the three preceding reigns and reproducing the very words of the warnings given in each

debates.question: Is the promise attached to obedience a real reprieve?

positions.view: yes, a plain conditional: an uninterrupted succession in state and tranquillity, since the most effectual way to preserve the dignity of government is to do the duty of it

no: the exile was already determined and had to be borne, and what repentance could still secure was a shorter and milder captivity with some form of the kingdom surviving, which is mitigation and not impunity

outliers.reading: Distinguishes the pair in the charge, judgment condemning the guilty and justice acquitting the innocent, and finds the specification that follows taking them in reverse order; then explains why the same three helpless classes are always named, since a judge who cannot be swayed by relations or by wealth in their case proves his integrity conspicuously.

Notes that the verb of the charge differs from the one used in the previous chapter and implies a less formal act, and settles from the context that the house doomed by the oath is the palace and not the Temple.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and speak there this word,
And say, Hear the word of the Lord, O king of Judah, that sittest upon the throne of David, thou, and thy servants, and thy people that enter in by these gates:

Thus saith the Lord; Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor: and do no wrong, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow, neither shed innocent blood in this place.
For if ye do this thing indeed, then shall there enter in by the gates of this house kings sitting upon the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, he, and his servants, and his people.
But if ye will not hear these words, I swear by myself, saith the Lord, that this house shall become a desolation.

6.pericope_label: Thou art Gilead unto me, and the head of Lebanon: yet surely I will make thee a wilderness; and many nations shall pass by this city, and they shall say, Wherefore hath the Lord done thus unto this great city?

schools.summary: Reads the comparison as poetry, locating its point in the forests that crowned both heights, and carries the metaphor forward so that the felled cedars are the princes and counsellors as well as the timber.

Refuses the received reading of the comparison and makes it a warning by precedent drawn from the fate of the northern kingdom, while insisting that the destroyers are consecrated instruments and not merely enemies.
Works from the geography of the two regions and from the fertility and height that made them emblems of the royal house, and keeps the felling as a picture of the country's ruin.

debates.question: What does the comparison to Gilead and the head of Lebanon assert?

positions.view: the splendour and elevation of the royal house, Lebanon being the highest mountain and Gilead the richest country, with perhaps a glance at the oaks and cedars the palace was built from
the forests crowning both heights, the oaks of the one district as famous as the cedars of the other and both fit symbols of sovereign glory

not a compliment but a warning by precedent: Gilead stands by a part for the northern kingdom, already wholly depopulated, and the head of Lebanon for Jerusalem, so that the sense is that Jerusalem shall be to God what Gilead already is

debates.question: What are the choice cedars that are to be felled?

positions.view: the princes of the royal house with the chief counsellors and generals, as well as the columns of cedar wood
a forest scene standing for the country's destruction, a multitude of fellers each with his axe and no resistance offered
either the cedar-panelled chambers or the trees of the mountain, and in either case whatever was splendid in the city

outliers.reading: Draws from the Hebrew of the appointment, which says the Lord will sanctify the destroyers, not only that they are appointed but that what they do by his order is consistent with his holiness.

Collates the versions on the verb of appointment, which render it as bringing, sanctifying, preparing and commissioning, and argues that the noun for the destroyers' equipment means an implement of any kind, so that hatchet suits it better than weapon.

themes: For thus saith the Lord unto the king’s house of Judah; Thou art Gilead unto me, and the head of Lebanon: yet surely I will make thee a wilderness, and cities which are not inhabited.
And I will prepare destroyers against thee, every one with his weapons: and they shall cut down thy choice cedars, and cast them into the fire.
And many nations shall pass by this city, and they shall say every man to his neighbour, Wherefore hath the Lord done thus unto this great city?
Then they shall answer, Because they have forsaken the covenant of the Lord their God, and worshipped other gods, and served them.

10.pericope_label: Weep ye not for the dead, but weep sore for him that goeth away: for thus saith the Lord touching Shallum the son of Josiah, He shall die in the place whither they have led him captive, and shall see this land no more

schools.summary: Marks the verse as the opening of a detailed review of three reigns, accounts for the private name by its meaning and its ill associations, and argues from the silence of the later history that the prediction held.
Declines to tie the lament to named individuals and extends it to the whole people, and uses the succession to insist that a pious ancestor shields nobody.
Identifies the exile from the historical books and follows him from his deposition to his death in Egypt.
Reads the reversal of mourning as a lesson about envying the dying and pitying the living, and traces the people's own part in setting up the king who fell.

debates.question: Is the command about weeping addressed to particular kings or to the people generally?

positions.view: to two named kings, the dead being Josiah and the departing one his deposed successor
a general declaration about the whole people, since exile would be a slow infection consuming them and death the better lot, with any allusion to the two standing inside that wider sense

debates.question: Who is the Shallum of the oracle?

positions.view: Jehoahaz, against the identifications with Zedekiah and with Jeconiah proposed by earlier commentators
Jehoahaz under his name before the throne, as his brothers also took new names on their accession

Jehoahaz, the private name being preferred because it means retribution and would have seemed of ill augury for a short and disastrous reign, recalling an Israelite king of that name who reigned a single month
Jehoahaz, whom the people had set up over an elder brother, so that his deposition within three months exposed the folly of their preference
Jeconiah rather, called son of Josiah by the Hebrew usage that names descendants sons

outliers.reading: Observes that the second verb of the command means to nod, and that the head was shaken in scorn as readily as in condolence.

Argues from silence that the prediction held, since the exile's name is absent from the whole of the following history and there is no trace of his being alive even when the prophet was himself dragged down into Egypt.

themes: Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country.
For thus saith the Lord touching Shallum the son of Josiah king of Judah, which reigned instead of Josiah his father, which went forth out of this place; He shall not return thither any more:
But he shall die in the place whither they have led him captive, and shall see this land no more.

13.pericope_label: Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, that useth his neighbour service without wages: did not thy father do judgment and justice? was not this to know me? saith the Lord

schools.summary: Supplies the social setting of the forced labour and the technical detail of the building, presses the verb of the taunt for its sense of vying, and reads the praise of the father as praise of a healthy enjoyment joined to just rule.
Separates two wrongs the versions had run together, enslaving without cause and withholding wages, and turns the whole into an argument that cruelty proves religion rooted out.
Uses the charges to explain a taxation the histories record without explaining, and reduces the taunt to a question about what makes a man a great king.

debates.question: What is the force of the taunt about cedar?

positions.view: false security: the wainscot is no fortification and may be broken up or burnt
self-importance: whether a man is a great king because he lives in a splendid house
the verb means to vie, so the sense is that his ambition is in cedar and he is reproached for outdoing his greatest predecessors
not whether he will reign long but whether he supposes himself a king at all, since kingship consists in administering right and justice and not in raising palaces
derision of a foolish confidence, a man painting walls when he had many dangers to dread
money ill got or diverted, with materials and workmen left unpaid
the mechanism of a heavy taxation the histories record without explaining: he took the hirelings' wages and set the people to work for nothing
a revival of the forced labour of Solomon's day, pressing now on Israelites rather than resident foreigners, and an instance of despotism generally
two distinct wrongs the versions have run together, enslaving a neighbour for no cause, which is the wrong judgment, and giving him nothing for his work, which is the injustice

outliers.reading: Presses a comparison further than anyone else: a robber who kills at least takes the spoil, but the man who extorts a poor man's labour and then sends him away naked and needy has done the more atrocious of the two.

Finds the verb for cutting the windows to be the one used of dilating the eyes with antimony, so that unusual width is meant, and supposes the whole project driven by a vainglorious wish to imitate the king who had set this one on his throne.

themes: Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour’s service without wages, and giveth him not for his work;
That saith, I will build me a wide house and large chambers, and cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion.
Shalt thou reign, because thou closest thyself in cedar? did not thy father eat and drink, and do judgment and justice, and then it was well with him?
He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well with him: was not this to know me? saith the Lord.
But thine eyes and thine heart are not but for thy covetousness, and for to shed innocent blood, and for oppression, and for violence, to do it.

18.pericope_label: They shall not lament for him, saying, Ah my brother! or, Ah his glory! He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem

schools.summary: Treats the quoted cries as the formulas of professional mourners and reconstructs the unburied end from the later form of the same threat and from the movements of the captive train.
Reads the cries as a scheme of lament and condolence, presses the participle for dragging rather than carrying, and builds a doctrine of burial that it then qualifies against itself.
Documents the funeral refrain from living custom elsewhere and reduces the sentence to its essential, that none attended and none mourned.

debates.question: Whose glory is lamented in the quoted cries?

positions.view: the queen's: the last word is feminine, and the four cries divide into lament for the dead king and condolence for the surviving widow whose glory departed with her husband
probably neither, since sister would not fit a king: the words are more likely a chorus of mourners, male and female, calling to one another
the professional formulas of hired mourners engaged for men and women alike, one of which the Greek found objectionable and dropped

debates.question: How was the burial of an ass carried out?

positions.view: left unburied in the open field or thrown into a flaying-ground, the body dragged out beyond the gates
cast into a ditch as any brute is, and left to the dogs
no direct record survives, but the king was dragged off in chains with the captives and probably died on the road, his corpse left where it fell as the army moved on
he probably died in fetters at Jerusalem before removal and was then dragged out of the city in the conqueror's indignation at his rebellion

outliers.reading: Explains how such a refrain works by quoting a traveller's record of laments heard in India, a mother's for her child and a daughter's for her mother, in which every line closes on the same repeated cry.

Warns that the prophet describes the custom of his age without approving it, as he had described royal chariots without approving an ostentation kings had been forbidden, and judges such lamentation a theatrical madness; then qualifies his own doctrine that lack of burial is a curse, since God has let faithful servants lie unburied and outward circumstances often will not distinguish the good from the bad.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah; They shall not lament for him, saying, Ah my brother! or, Ah sister! they shall not lament for him, saying, Ah lord! or, Ah his glory!
He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem.

20.pericope_label: Go up to Lebanon, and cry: I spake unto thee in thy prosperity, but thou saidst, I will not hear. O inhabitant of Lebanon, that makest thy nest in the cedars, how gracious shalt thou be when pangs come upon thee

schools.summary: Reads the mountains as witnesses overlooking the invader's march, gives the literal plural of the word for prosperity and the sense of careless security it carries, and catches the play between the wind that feeds and the shepherds who fed.
Takes the summons as pure irony and sustains a marriage figure through the passage, God the husband and the neighbouring powers the lovers, refusing to soften the verb of hearing into obeying.
Reads the geography as pointing toward the allies from whom help was expected, or as the route of the deportation itself, and hears the closing question as a strong irony.
Traces the nation through haughtiness in peace, terror at the alarm, and tameness under pressure, and hears in the last phrase the piety that pain produces and does not outlast.

debates.question: Why are the three mountains named?

positions.view: as high ground from which a cry might carry, Jerusalem calling to her neighbours for help
because these heights lay along the road by which the captives were to be led out
as witnesses overlooking the invader's line of march, the people called from the counterfeit forest of their cedar palaces to the real mountains
because they look toward the allies from whom help was expected, who are themselves already in the conqueror's hand
as pure irony, a command to cry where crying is useless, addressed to people past counsel

debates.question: What does the closing question about being gracious mean?

positions.view: read it rather as how wilt thou groan, tied to the pangs of travail that follow
keep the received text: it is plain irony and needs no variant
a forecast of the piety that pain produces, the humbling and the promises of amendment that do not outlast the pangs

outliers.reading: Digresses from the figure to insist that the mountain has real inhabitants, with villages, a convent and a valley of hermitages, before returning to say that Jerusalem is nevertheless meant.

Sustains a marriage figure that no one else presses: God is the husband and the neighbouring powers are the lovers, the simplicity of faith being our spiritual chastity, so that looking about for safety is adultery; and a husband who warned in time and confirmed his counsel by kindness leaves the wife who is unmoved by both without excuse.

themes: Go up to Lebanon, and cry; and lift up thy voice in Bashan, and cry from the passages: for all thy lovers are destroyed.
I spake unto thee in thy prosperity; but thou saidst, I will not hear. This hath been thy manner from thy youth, that thou obeyedst not my voice.
The wind shall eat up all thy pastors, and thy lovers shall go into captivity: surely then shalt thou be ashamed and confounded for all thy wickedness.
O inhabitant of Lebanon, that makest thy nest in the cedars, how gracious shalt thou be when pangs come upon thee, the pain as of a woman in travail!

24.pericope_label: Though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence: O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord; write ye this man childless, for no man of his seed shall prosper

schools.summary: Sets out the forms of the king's name and dates the oracle from the grammar, corrects the word behind the broken thing, identifies the register the command to write is addressed to, and keeps the question of actual childlessness open.
Reads the clipped name and the ironical questions as instruments against a confidence in the throne, and alone reconciles the sentence with the promise of an unbroken line.
Assigns the exclamation over the broken thing to the people or to God speaking through the prophet, and treats the entry in the genealogical tables as the plain sense of writing him childless.

debates.question: Who speaks the question about the broken thing?

positions.view: the people, exclaiming when they heard the sentence pronounced
the prophet, identifying himself with those who looked on so young a man's doom with wonder and pity while still pronouncing it inevitable
the prophet, feigning astonishment at a thing monstrous so that others might cease to wonder
the prophet, speaking in the person of God

debates.question: To whom is the command to write him childless addressed?

positions.view: to angels or to prophets, as some hold, or else impersonally
to the scribes who kept the register of the royal genealogies, told to enter the name without waiting for his death
to no one in particular: the phrase is drawn from the practice of recording lasting decrees on public tablets, and its point is permanence

outliers.reading: Alone faces the difficulty the sentence raises against the promise of an unbroken line, and answers that the childlessness is confined to the interval before Christ: grace was hidden for a time but never extinguished, as the Church itself was later invisible and yet not dead.

Holds it certain that the sceptre departed in this king, since not even Zerubbabel sat on the throne, but doubts whether he died childless in fact, since in these genealogies adoption and levirate marriage so constantly replace parentage that nothing can be inferred.

themes: As I live, saith the Lord, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence;

And I will give thee into the hand of them that seek thy life, and into the hand of them whose face thou fearest, even into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of the Chaldeans.
And I will cast thee out, and thy mother that bare thee, into another country, where ye were not born; and there shall ye die.
But to the land whereunto they desire to return, thither shall they not return.
Is this man Coniah a despised broken idol? is he a vessel wherein is no pleasure? wherefore are they cast out, he and his seed, and are cast into a land which they know not?
O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord.
Thus saith the Lord, Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah.
